title: Cryptorchidism
subject: Pathology
summary: Undescended testis fails to reach the scrotum, affecting ~1% of one‑year‑old boys. It leads to tubular atrophy, infertility and a 3‑5‑fold rise in testicular cancer risk, even in the contralateral descended testis.

sections.p: Cryptorchidism is the failure of one or both testes to complete their normal descent from the abdomen into the scrotum by the time of birth or early infancy.

faq.a: It preserves spermatogenesis, reduces tubular atrophy, and lowers the risk of testicular cancer.

faq.q: Can a testis that never descends still produce testosterone?
faq.a: Yes, Leydig cells often function, so hormonal levels may be normal in early childhood.
A family history increases risk, but most cases are sporadic.

exam: What is the next step when a 6‑month‑old boy has an empty right scrotum but a palpable inguinal mass? — Perform an inguinal ultrasound if available; otherwise arrange prompt surgical referral for orchidopexy.

How does cryptorchidism increase testicular cancer risk, and what surveillance is advised? — Atrophic tubules develop intratubular germ‑cell neoplasia; counsel annual self‑exam after puberty and consider ultrasound if any abnormality.
A bilateral undescended testis is found in a newborn with Prune‑belly syndrome. Which associated problem must you look for? — Obstructive uropathy (hydronephrosis) due to urinary tract malformation.

Why is high‑dose testosterone therapy not the first treatment for an undescended testis? — It does not reliably induce descent and may suppress the hypothalamic‑pituitary axis, worsening future fertility.

In a low‑resource clinic without ultrasound, how would you confirm the location of an undescended testis? — Use careful palpation of the inguinal canal and abdomen; if not felt, refer for surgical exploration.
What red‑flag symptom would change management from elective orchidopexy to emergency surgery? — Sudden severe scrotal or groin pain with vomiting suggests torsion, requiring immediate detorsion.
How does prematurity influence the timing of orchidopexy? — Premature infants have delayed descent; surgery is still aimed before 18 months corrected age to optimise outcomes.
Explain why the contralateral descended testis also carries increased cancer risk. — Shared embryologic and hormonal environment predisposes both testes; surveillance must include the normal testis.
